pages.x: In 827 a rebel Byzantine admiral, Euphemius, invited the Aghlabid emirs of Tunisia into Sicily. An army of about 10,000 men landed at Mazara under an aged judge and scholar, Asad ibn al-Furat. He died besieging Syracuse, but the invaders stayed, and in 831 took Palermo.

The conquest went on fortress by fortress through the mountains for 75 years. Arab raiders also struck mainland Italy, and in 846 even plundered the church of St Peter outside the walls of Rome. Enna, the island's central stronghold, fell in 859, and Syracuse in 878, after a siege of nine months.

By 965 the last Byzantine towns had fallen. Under its emirs Sicily flourished: the Arabs brought lemons, oranges, sugar cane and cotton, and new ways to water the land, and Palermo, with hundreds of mosques, became one of the largest cities in Europe.

In 1038, while the emirs fought among themselves, the Byzantine general George Maniakes invaded, with Norman knights in his army and Varangian guards led by Harald Hardrada, the future king of Norway. He took Messina and Syracuse, but was recalled under suspicion, and his gains were soon lost.

Normans from northern France had come south as mercenaries, and stayed as conquerors. The boldest was Robert de Hauteville, called Guiscard, the Cunning. He beat a papal army in 1053, was made duke of Apulia and Calabria by the pope, and in 1071 took Bari, ending five centuries of Byzantine rule in Italy.

Robert's youngest brother, Roger, crossed to Sicily in 1061 at the invitation of one of the quarrelling emirs, and took Messina. In 1063, with a small band of knights, he beat a far larger Muslim army at Cerami, and in 1072 the brothers took Palermo by land and sea.

It took Roger almost twenty more years to win the rest. Noto, the last Muslim town, surrendered in 1091, the year he also took Malta. As count of Sicily he let his Muslim subjects keep their faith, and Arab scholars, Greek monks and Latin knights lived side by side under Norman rule.

In Palermo, Roger's son, King Roger II, built a chapel for his palace in the 1140s, with Greek mosaics of Christ, Latin inscriptions, and a wooden ceiling carved and painted by Muslim artists, with writing in Arabic. It sums up the kingdom of three cultures.

The Norman conquests became the Kingdom of Sicily in 1130, one of the richest states in Europe, where Arab, Greek and Latin learning met. Sicilian is still full of Arabic words, and Arab gardens, Byzantine mosaics and Norman churches stand side by side in Palermo.
pts: The Arabs took Sicily over 75 years
The Normans took it from 1061 to 1091
